title: Cap. IX Arg. 6 Sol cont.: Thomas — free will disordered toward evil cannot offer no impediment to grace; God sometimes converts even those who impede; the difference hangs on simple will
pass_a_gloss: Thomas philosophizes much better of this matter, who teaches that in free will inclined unto evil by a preceding inordination, it is not seated that it should offer no impediment unto Divine grace, Contra Gent. l. 3. c. 160. Then he adds, cap. 161. that God nevertheless sometimes from the abundance of his goodness turns even those who offer an impediment unto grace away from evil, and converts them unto good. At length he also adds that this is done in those alone in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice may be manifested. But of this discrimination, why he converts these putting an obstacle, others he does not convert, the reason is not to be sought, because it depends upon his simple will. In vain therefore does Corvinus impugn reprobation from this, that God is prepared to give richer grace unto all those who so use received grace that they do whatsoever by it they can do, since no one performs this, and since this very thing, not finally to oppose an obstacle unto Divine grace, flows from election, and does not precede election.
pass_b_english: Thomas reasons far better here. He teaches that free will, already disordered toward evil, is not so set that it offers no impediment to divine grace (Contra Gent. 3.160). Then (cap. 161) he adds that God nonetheless sometimes, from abundance of his goodness, turns even those who impede grace away from evil and converts them to good — and that this happens only in those in whom he wills his mercy to appear, so that in all others the order of justice is shown. Why he converts these who put an obstacle and not others is not to be sought; it hangs on his simple will. So Corvinus vainly attacks reprobation from God's readiness to give richer grace to all who use received grace so as to do whatever they can by it — since no one does that, and since not finally opposing an obstacle to divine grace itself flows from election and does not precede election.
source_text: Multo melius hac de re philosophatur Thomas, qui docet, in libero arbitrio per inordinationem praecedentem ad malum inclinato, non esse situm ut nullum impedimentum gratiae Divinae praestet, Contra Gent. l. 3. c. 160. Deinde adjungit, cap. 161. Deum tamen interdum ex abundantia bonitatis suae eos etiam qui impedimentum gratiae praestant, avertere a malo, et convertere ad bonum. Tandem et illud addit, Hoc fieri in illis solis, in quibus vult suam misericordiam apparere, ita quod in aliis omnibus justitiae ordo manifestetur. Hujus autem discriminis, quare hos ponentes obicem convertat, alios non convertat, rationem inquirendam non esse, quia dependet ex simplici ejus voluntate. Frustra igitur Corvinus ex eo reprobationem impugnat, quod Deus paratus sit uberiorem gratiam dare illis omnibus, qui ita utuntur gratia accepta, ut faciant quodcunque per eam possunt facere, cum nemo hoc praestet, et cum hoc ipsum, non finaliter opponere obicem gratiae Divinae, ex electione dimanet, non autem praecedat electionem.
